articles.title: What happened to AAP’s ‘clean governance’ claim? A CAG report expose
articles.description: New Delhi: The latest CAG report on Delhi is damaging for the Aam Aadmi Party for a simple reason: it questions the very governance model Arvind Kejriwal sold to voters for years. The Comptroller and Auditor General of India report, tabled in the Delhi Assembly on August 7, covered major areas of government functioning between 2018 and 2023. Its findings point to more than Rs 2,030 crore in quantified irregularities. Beyond that number, the audit flagged GST transactions running into tens of thousands of crores where enforcement and scrutiny were found wanting. For a government that built its politics around clean administration, technology and efficient delivery, the problem is not one isolated lapse. The CAG found weaknesses across tax collection, electricity subsidies, government tenders and departmental spending. GST red flags were everywhere, but checks were almost absent The most serious findings came from GST administration. The audit found taxpayers generating E-Way bills showing large movement of goods while either filing nil tax returns or not filing returns at all. Five taxpayers generated 759 E-Way bills involving supplies worth Rs 33.89 crore but filed nil GSTR-3B returns. Tax of Rs 4.68 crore remained unpaid. Another 15 taxpayers generated 580 E-Way bills involving Rs 252.66 crore and tax liability of Rs 31.46 crore without filing GSTR-3B returns. Even businesses whose registrations had been cancelled continued generating E-Way bills. Twenty-eight cancelled taxpayers generated 3,629 E-Way bills involving Rs 734.75 crore, carrying tax implications of Rs 99.39 crore. According to the audit, assessment action did not follow. The wider numbers were much bigger. The CAG found 8,334 cancelled taxpayers generating E-Way bills worth Rs 68,680.88 crore. Another 4,076 non-filers generated bills worth Rs 11,635.36 crore. Yet only 0.10 per cent of total E-Way bills were verified. That is the core problem in plain language: the system was producing warning signs, but the government machinery was barely checking them. A detailed audit of just 70 taxpayers found 344 instances of non-compliance with revenue implications of Rs 3,071.92 crore. Power subsidy reached connections that used no power Electricity subsidy was one of AAP’s biggest political selling points. The CAG did not question the idea of subsidy itself. It questioned how loosely it was administered. Delhi’s electricity subsidy bill rose from Rs 2,405.59 crore in 2019-20 to Rs 3,161 crore in 2022-23. The scheme covered roughly 80 per cent of domestic consumers, but the audit found no strong socio-economic targeting behind the 400-unit threshold. More damagingly, subsidy money was paid even to connections showing zero electricity consumption. More than 50,000 consumers with no consumption for over 12 months received Rs 17.81 crore. Over 90,000 consumers with zero consumption for six to 11 months received another Rs 11.88 crore. More than 1.7 lakh consumers with zero consumption for three to five months received Rs 12.57 crore. In all, Rs 42.26 crore went to dormant domestic connections between 2019 and 2023. The political problem for AAP is obvious. A subsidy projected as targeted relief was being paid even where there was no recorded electricity use for months. Government tenders throw up even bigger questions The e-procurement findings are equally uncomfortable. Online tendering is supposed to make government contracts more transparent and reduce the possibility of manipulation. The audit found 1,185 tenders were still floated manually despite an online system being available. It also found patterns that should have triggered immediate scrutiny. Forty-five tenders worth Rs 530.25 crore received bids from entities sharing the same PAN. In 38 tenders worth Rs 2.52 crore, all bids came from the same email ID. More than 14,500 bids relating to 7,181 tenders worth Rs 3,217.44 crore originated from common IP addresses. Most strikingly, in 2,519 tenders worth Rs 2,114.87 crore, the same IP address was used by bidders as well as departmental users. That does not by itself prove that every tender was fixed. But these are not routine clerical mistakes either. They are exactly the kind of digital footprints an e-procurement system is supposed to detect. The CAG also found departmental users logging into the system even after retirement, financial bids being decrypted before technical evaluation, incomplete contract-award records and short bidding periods. Only 3.47 per cent of tenders had complete award details recorded. More than 1.54 lakh tenders worth over Rs 1 lakh crore passed through the system during the audited period. Rs 29 crore spent on land lying unused for 17 years The report also documented smaller examples of administrative waste. The Delhi State Industrial and Infrastructure Development Corporation spent Rs 29.45 crore on 81.42 acres of land at Baprola that remained unused for over 17 years. The Public Works Department made avoidable payments of Rs 5.63 crore. Delayed investment of DTC EPF Trust funds potentially cost Rs 5.50 crore in interest. GTB Hospital incurred Rs 1.93 crore in avoidable payments, while procedural lapses at the Delhi Jal Board led to another Rs 1.56 crore in avoidable expenditure. The CAG also recorded revenue arrears exceeding Rs 70,000 crore, with 65 per cent pending for more than five years.

articles.title: From CWG 2026 Glory to Asian Games 2026: India’s Sporting rise creates fresh hopes for greater International success
articles.description: The Commonwealth Games (CWG) 2026, which began on July 23, 2026, came to a glittering close on August 2-3, 2026, at Glasgow, the capital city of Scotland (UK). The Indian contingent did its best under the circumstances and brought home 39 medals, including 13 gold, 17 silver and 9 bronze. The flag and baton of the CWG were handed over to the Indian officials at the end of the closing ceremony in recognition of the fact that the next CWG in 2030 would be held in India at Ahmedabad. The Indian Olympic Association President, P.T.Usha, Javelin Throw Champion, Neeraj Chopra and the Dy. Chief Minister of Gujarat, Harsh Sanghavi received the flag and the baton with the deserved honour and protocol of the Games. This handover officially marked India taking charge to host the 2030 historic Centenary Commonwealth Games in Ahmedabad. The first such games were held in Hamilton, Canada, in 1930. Hosting the 2030 Games is expected to boost India’s global sporting profile, accelerate world-class sports infrastructure development, and showcase the country’s organisational capabilities on the international stage. It should also be seen particularly in the context of the preparations for the Asian Games to be held in September this year in Japan, followed by the Olympics to be held in the US in 2028. India had sent a contingent of 191 members headed by Chief de Mission Rohit Rajpal and Deputy Chief de Mission Ravi Bengani. The contingent included 126 athletes (77 men and 49 women) and 51 team officials to participate in the games. Those who participated included 32 competitors (22 men and 10 women) in Athletics, 15 representatives each in Boxing & Judo and 12 competitors in weightlifting. There were only 10 sports disciplines plus the para sports this time, which surely impacted the results for India as well. Shooting, wrestling, archery, hockey, badminton and table tennis -the mainstay sports of India, which bring a lot of fortunes for it traditionally, were not included in the games this time. Ever since the inception of CWG in 1930, India continued to participate in the games barring only three times, including the first one. It got the best results in the CWG 2010 when the games were organised in Delhi. It stood second in the medal tally with 101 total medals, including 38 gold, 27 silver and 36 bronze. The second best performance by India was in CWG 2002 at Manchester when it won 30 gold, 22 silver, 17 bronze with a total of 69 medals. The performance this time at Glasgow with a tally of 39 medals was also satisfactory and encouraging. It secured 5th place on the overall medal table of the games and the first place among the Asian countries in the CWG 2026. This time, the boxers from India exhibited great class and character and made history by entering the final 10 events of the discipline. They won seven finals and also got 7 gold medals and 3 silver medals. This is India’s best-ever boxing performance. The gold finishers for India included Jasmine Lamboria, Preeti Pawar, Sakshi Chaudhary, Priya Ghanghas, Arundhati Chaudhary, Sachin Siwach and Ankush Panghal. The champion weightlifter Mirabai Chanu secured gold in the 48kg women’s category. In this way, she was able to successfully achieve a historic third consecutive CWG title. Also Read: Who is Annapurni Subramaniam? Astrophysicist who became first Indian woman to receive the COSPAR Vikram Sarabhai Medal Sharmila Dhankar won gold in the women’s shot-put F57, leading the record-making campaign for Indian para-athletes. Dilip Gavit won a historic gold in the men’s 100m T47 event with a game record time of 10.71 seconds. This is the men’s first-ever para-athletic gold at the CWG. Mohammed Basil got silver in the same category, thus giving India a 1-2 finish in the finals. While Soman Rana won gold in the men’s shot-put F57 para-athlete event, Shubham Juyal got a silver medal in the same event. Shilpa Shyla secured a bronze medal in the women’s shot-put F57 para-athlete event following a successful appeal. Gulveer Singh created a new history and became the first Indian track and field athlete to win two individual medals at a single CWG (silver in 10,000m and bronze in 5,000m). The ace champion Neeraj Chopra, alongside debutant Yash Vir Singh, won silver and bronze respectively in the Javelin throw. Asmita Dey and Harsh Singh clinched the first-ever gold in the Judo competition, marking India’s strong entry into the elite club of the sportsmen and women of the discipline. These remarkable achievements of India at an international platform are a reflection of the sports policy of India coupled with the infrastructure development at a grassroots level. Training methodology, investment in the sports sector and the grooming of sportsmen and women at a tender age are the basics for the development of sports in the modern context. Then there are centres for sportsmen and women in a number of states in India where special arrangements have been made to groom the budding talent under national and international experts of various games and sports. A number of the athletes revealed that they were fully supported by their state governments and also the big institutions in the country. Great international players like Virat Kohli have also sponsored some key athletes who have shown exemplary results. The scenario in India has drastically changed and improved in the context of the athletes taking part in international competitions like CWG, Asian Games, Olympics and other important competitions held intermittently. Big companies and other organisations have been coming forward to help and support the deserving talent in the country. The CWG overall medal table highlights the most successful nations in the history of the competition. Australia continues to lead the all-time standings with an incredible 2,773 medals, followed by England and Canada, while India proudly holds fourth place with 602 medals. The rankings reflect decades of excellence across multiple sports and generations of world-class athletes. Keeping in view the next CWG 2030, the Government of India, [...]

articles.title: Beginning of the End
articles.description: 73 years down the line, Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah’s unceremonious ouster, on August 9, 1953, as the prime minister of (autonomous) Jammu & Kashmir state, stands out as the single most consequential event in its history since the state’s accession to the Indian Union on October 26, 1947. Logically, history would mark the event as one of the most undemocratic, immoral and unconstitutional acts. And in political terms, it proved to be—as indeed it was designed--an irreversible shift of power balance between Srinagar and New Delhi, to the former’s crushing disadvantage. It took 66 long years to carry the ‘process’ to its ultimate logical conclusion--- on August 5, 2019; when the border state was physically ripped apart and unprecedently downgraded in its constitutional status from a semi-autonomous state to a power-less Union Territory. The chemistry of the two events— ‘1953 & 2019’—though more than half a century apart--establishes the fact of their being linked by a discernible umbilical cord. The amorphous post-1953 politico-constitutional structure inherently carried the seeds of an unwritten, logical built-in provision for a more drastic inevitable conclusion. Only that it took so long coming--on August 5, 2019. New Delhi-based Observer Research Foundation (ORF) recently published (declassified) J&K-related official documents pertaining to behind-the-curtain activities within the corridors of power in New Delhi and Srinagar, before and after the Sheikh’s dismissal and arrest on August 9, 1953. One of the emphatic conclusions obtained from these documents is that, long before the Jan Sangh/BJP, it was none other than prime minister Jawahar Lal Nehru himself who had set his eyes upon getting rid of Art 370 lock, stock and barrel. He often said ‘ghiste, ghiste ghis jaye ga’ (wear and tear will consume it). But he did not rest at that. There was method in the madness of ‘1953’. Dispensing with its physical symbol in flesh and blood, the then prime minister Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah, thus became a compelling casualty in the process. Nehru’s task was made easier by Abdullah’s misplaced over-confidence in his own indispensability. Towards the fag end of his first phase in power, Sheikh started biting more than he could chew, making it easier for his mightier foe. That also partly explains how Nehru managed to achieve his objective at an affordable political cost. Sheikh’s shrewd successor, Bakhshi Ghulam Mohammad was able to walkout with the former’s almost entire legislative flock and also install a parallel, durable political superstructure on the ground that served his purpose adequately. He appeared to be in command even as he was atrociously rough with a strident irrepressible popular undercurrent. After New Delhi accomplished its immediate objective it was the turn of the Sheikh’s successor to be pushed towards hastening the follow-up: (1) Winding up the state’s parallel constituent assembly after seeking its endorsement on finality of the state’s accession with India and (2) dismantling the jarring constitutional ‘oddities’---the nomenclature of the head of the state as Sadr-i-Riyasat and that of the Prime Minister of J&K. However, while Bakhshi readily obliged on the first, he appeared to be dragging his feet over the second proposition. His conduct attracted suspicion in New Delhi. He was put under watch. Like his tall predecessor, Bakhshi began to feel the heat under his feet. But, unlike Sheikh’s tactlessness, Bakhshi countered by erecting tactical defences on his home ground. By 1957, New Delhi had begun to get impatient with Bakhshi whose pre-occupation with his own survival on his home ground induced him to rework his priorities. Nehru sought to checkmate Bakhshi within their camp by inducing the formation of a parallel outfit, Democratic National Conference (DNC), led by Ghulam Mohammad Sadiq and including Syed Mir Qasim and DP Dhar. That, among other matters, sparked a running internal battle over the fate of Art 370; most of it beyond the public view. The ORF documents quoted GM Sadiq as taking the position that “Art 370 offered only illusory notions of autonomy and if ‘those in Delhi’ felt the time had come to end it, we should not begrudge it. Personally, I believe it gave no particular advantage except for creating a psychological barrier between Kashmir and the rest of India”. Mir Qasim was quoted as having maintained that “except for the right of permanent citizenship—mainly property rights—it (Art 370) offered little real benefit. Bringing the state on a par with the rest of the country, particularly in labour laws, would work to the advantage of our general population.” Both Sadiq and Mir Qasim favoured “same administrative and organisational pattern as in the rest of the country’. Bakhshi’s survival strategy eventually pushed him to the opposite end of this one-upmanship. He used Art 370 as a political shield to ward off threat to his position at the helm. ‘This battle will be fought openly in the fields and farms of Kashmir and not secretly in the corridors of power”, became his war cry. At one point, Bakhshi went to the extreme when he sought to equate the then Union home minister, Lal Bahadur Shastri, with Jana Sangh leader Balraj Madhok for what he had stated on the floor of the Parliament in reply to a question by a Jana Sangh MP. His local detractors were quick to jump at it and cry foul: ‘Bakhshi is following the Sheikh’s path’. The end result was that New Delhi’s discreet swipe at Art 370 fell through and Bakhshi managed to survive; though not for long. A few months down the line, Bakhshi’s over-confidence impelled him to miscalculate and walk straight into Nehru’s parlour. It was in 1963 that Nehru floated his ‘Kamaraj Plan’ named after the then Congress president K Kamaraj. The plan had been devised to weed out a few corrupt top Congressmen from power who had become a political liability. Bakhshi, not being a Congress member, did not come within its ambit. But his (fatal) misplaced confidence in his ‘indispensability’ impelled him to instantly purchase a 4-Anna Congress membership ticket and foolishly tender his resignation; not even imagining its acceptance. To nobody’s surprise but his own, Bakhshi found himself among the few whose resignation had been accepted. His political capital earned on his home ground (Kashmir) over his pro-Art 370 stance was washed out in the public fury sparked by the mysterious theft of Holy Relic from Hazratbal Shrine in 1963. Its immediate emotional fallout put a brake on any further attempt at Art 370. Even so, Bakhshi’s bete noir-successor GM Sadiq managed to create space for its substantial erosion. The nomenclature of the head of the state was changed from Sadar-i-Riyasat to Governor and that of the (J&K’s) prime minister to chief minister. The ruling National Conference wound its separate shop by merging into the Congress. By the way, GM Sadiq achieved the (dubious?) distinction of being the only state leader to have served both, as the prime minister and the chief minister. J&K’s separate constitution was substantially eroded with the torrent-like inflow of central laws and key administrative changes, emaciating and hollowing the Art 370. Yet, Bakhshi had so vitiated the ground conditions that New Delhi felt compelled to restrain itself and let its hollowed shell remain; until the BJP arrived on the scene, half a century later, to perform its last rites with disproportionate ‘shock and awe’. Retrospectively, an academic question arises that whether ‘August 5, 2019’ was possible to put through at such affordable cost, as it eventually it did, if ‘August 9, 1953’ had not happened. Presumably, no. However, there is an ironical twist in the story. It was a ‘tamed’ Sher-e-Kashmir, back in power in 1975 for his second and final innings. 22-year long political wilderness had taken its logical toll. So much so that in one of his weakest moments, precisely on March 13, 1981, the Sheikh made a stunning statement on the floor of the state Assembly in Jammu saying ‘Art 370 is not sacrosanct. It can be done away with if and when the it becomes necessary’. One view had it that the ‘voluntary’ offer was addressed to ‘New Delhi’ for endorsing the Kashmir leader’s dynastic succession plan, after having got rid of his commonly perceived ‘natural successor’ Mirza Afzal Beg in 1978 at no cost. Many years later the Congress, under Rajiv Gandhi’s leadership, tried to take a swipe. Around mid-March, 1986 the Congress decided that they had had enough of their unilateral support to Ghulam Mohammad Shah’s minority government without any reciprocity. PCC president, Mufti Mohammad Sayeed was conditionally offered the crown, at a high-level midnight meeting in New Delhi at which the acting Congress president Arjun Singh asked Mufti if he would be able to move a resolution in the state Assembly seeking abrogation of Art 370. Mufti pleaded his inability, saying that in the situation prevailing at that time any such move would backfire. That was the time when the Sarkaria Commission was half way through its assigned task to explore the possibility of devolution of powers from the centre to the states. Nevertheless, GM Shah’s ministry was sent packing with an overly eager Governor Jagmohan taking the reins. However, down the line, in 2015, it was Mufti who’s ill-fated ‘North Pole-South Pole alliance’, between his Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and the BJP, turned out to be the proverbial ‘camel’s nose into the Arab’s tent’. Today, Sheikh’s legacy effectively remains entombed with him near Hazratbal shrine on the banks of the Dal Lake. His third-generation dynastic successor is left with its pale shadow. Even though the historical context and political implications of August 9, 1953 coup against the Sheikh continue to evoke interest long after him, his own autobiography, ‘Aatish-e-Chinar’, only offers a partial, partisan account. The only surviving main actor of that drama, Dr Karan Singh’s published account doesn’t help either. Stray versions like that of Nehru’s personal assistant MO Mathai only endorse the perception that the plan was hatched at the highest level and that only a handful of top men from civil and military establishments were in the know. Mathai claims that Nehru had dictated a detailed note to him on July 30, 1953, ten days ahead of the ‘D-day’. Other players in the drama have let out stray bits and pieces. History continues to look for a convincing complete account. The final countdown was triggered on June 30, 1953 when the Jana Sangh founder, Syama Prasad Mukherji had died, under detention in Srinagar, for having crossed into J&K without a (mandatory) entry permit from the state government headed by the Sheikh. By then the atmospherics had been sufficiently vitiated, by escalating centre-state confrontation, to make the action against the Sheikh look inevitable; though not so drastic as it eventually turned out to be. In a way, Sheikh had made it easier for his wily tormentors with his reckless emotional outbursts rather than working out a proper counter survival strategy. Probably his unrivalled popularity on his home-ground blinded him to the machinations of a brute power. That explains how, at such critical juncture, he happened to be on a weekend break at Gulmarg resort, on the fateful day, where he found himself literally dragged from his bed, as well his throne, in the dead of night, caged and thrown into 22-year long political wilderness. Mohammad Sayeed Malik is a veteran journalist from Kashmir
